overview.title: 📖 Overview: Opening Chapter Six — Animals Disqualified From the Altar
overview.subtitle: Temurah 28a–28b
overview.hebrewSource: כָּל הָאֲסוּרִין לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ אוֹסְרִין בְּכׇל שֶׁהֵן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna opens Chapter Six with a list of animals permanently barred from the altar — those used in bestiality, set aside or worshipped as idols, given as payment to a prostitute or for a dog, crossbred, a tereifa, or born by caesarean section — and rules that even one such animal, mixed into any number of otherwise fit ones, disqualifies the entire group. The Gemara carefully distinguishes this ruling from two parallel mishnayot (in Zevaḥim and Avoda Zara) that might seem to say the same thing, explaining why each teaches something the others don't. It then works through the verse-by-verse derivation excluding each category from Leviticus 1:2's list of valid offering-animals, testing several attempted logical shortcuts (a fortiori inferences) that ultimately fail and require the Torah's own explicit exclusions. The daf closes with a debate over Gideon's seven-year-old bullock — was it actually worshipped, or merely set aside for future worship?

slides.title: 🚫 New Mishna: The Disqualified List
slides.subtitle: Any one of these, mixed in, ruins an unlimited quantity of otherwise-fit animals
rows: An animal that copulated with a person, in either direction
Set aside for idol worship — the animal itself is forbidden, but its ornaments may be sold to fund a real offering
Actually worshipped as an idol — both the animal AND its ornaments are forbidden (though it may still be eaten by people)
Given as payment to a prostitute, or as the price of a dog
Crossbred, fatally wounded, or born by caesarean section

callout.label: The mishna's core ruling:
callout.text: Unlike ordinary halakhic mixtures (where a minority is often nullified by a majority), even ONE such disqualified animal mixed among any number of fit ones renders the whole group unfit for the altar.

slides.title: 🔄 Why Isn't This Mishna Redundant?
slides.subtitle: Two parallel mishnayot seem to say the same thing — each earns its own place

steps.content: 1️⃣ A mishna in Zevaḥim already says mixtures with 'forbidden-to-benefit' items (dying sin offerings, a stoned ox) are never nullified — why repeat it here for merely 'disqualified-from-altar' items?
2️⃣ Answer: those are items whose very USE is forbidden; this mishna extends the rule even to items merely unfit for the ALTAR (but otherwise permitted to eat) — a real novelty

3️⃣ Further distinction (Rav Shimi bar Ashi): one mishna covers animals that mixed while ALREADY consecrated (repulsive to the altar); this one covers animals that mixed while still NON-SACRED, before consecration

4️⃣ A third parallel (Avoda Zara, on non-sacred items like idolatrous wine) is likewise needed — otherwise one might think only items 'repulsive to the Most High' resist nullification, while ordinary forbidden-benefit items among laypeople WOULD be nullified

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Each parallel mishna covers a distinct combination of variables (sacred/non-sacred timing, forbidden-to-use/merely-disqualified) — none is truly redundant.

slides.title: ⚖️ Excluding Robe'a and Nirva From the Altar
slides.subtitle: A tempting a fortiori inference, tested and partly rescued

lines.speaker: Proposed inference
lines.text: If a MERELY blemished animal (no transgression involved) is disqualified, shouldn't an animal used in BESTIALITY (an actual transgression) certainly be disqualified too?

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Not necessarily — an ox that plowed WITH a donkey (a real transgression) remains fully fit for the altar! So transgression alone doesn't disqualify.

lines.speaker: Refining the objection
lines.text: But that plowing violation carries no death penalty; bestiality DOES (for the human participant) — so the comparison may still work for capital-level transgressions.

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi's final limit
lines.text: Even this only works when the transgression was witnessed by TWO people (enabling capital punishment) — a verse ('from the cattle') is still needed to cover cases based on ONE witness or the owner's own admission, where no such stringency applies.

callout.label: Rabbi Shimon's parallel proof:
callout.text: He derives even the one-witness/admission case by his own a fortiori inference from a blemished animal (disqualified even by a single expert's ruling) — though the Rabbis still require the explicit verse.

slides.title: 📜 One Verse, Four Exclusions
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 1:2's phrase 'from the cattle, from the herd, or from the flock' does heavy lifting

boxes.title: Excluded by Context
items: 'From the CATTLE (behema)' → excludes rove'a/nirva — bestiality is described using this very word elsewhere (Lev. 20:15-16)
'From the HERD (bakar)' → excludes ne'evad — idol worship is described using 'ox' imagery (Psalms 106:19-20)

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon's Necessity Argument
items: 'From the FLOCK' → excludes muktzeh; the conjunction 'OR from the flock' → excludes an animal that gored a person

Why need BOTH rove'a and noge'ach excluded separately? Each has a unique stringency the other lacks (rove'a: even forced acts count; noge'ach: its owner pays a ransom) — so one exclusion couldn't imply the other

callout.label: Alternative derivation:
callout.text: The school of Rabbi Yishmael instead derives rove'a/ne'evad from the word 'מָשְׁחָתָם' ('their corruption') used for blemishes — since that term elsewhere always signals sexual immorality or idolatry — freeing up the cattle/herd/flock verse to exclude sick, old, or filthy animals instead.

slides.title: 🐂 Was Gideon's Bullock Actually Worshipped?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish's definition of 'muktzeh' tested against the biblical story

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: 'Muktzeh' means set aside specifically for SEVEN YEARS of future idol worship — proven from Gideon's father's 'second bullock of seven years' (Judges 6:25).

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But that bullock wasn't just SET ASIDE — it was reportedly actually WORSHIPPED already! That would make it 'ne'evad,' not merely 'muktzeh'!

lines.speaker: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov
lines.text: No — it was set aside FOR future worship, but never actually worshipped in practice.

lines.speaker: Rava's alternative
lines.text: Actually, it WAS worshipped — this was one of EIGHT normally-forbidden acts specially permitted to Gideon that very night (per Rabbi Abba bar Kahana), including slaughtering outside the Tabernacle, at night, and by a non-priest.

callout.label: Setting up the next daf:
callout.text: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana's list of eight extraordinary permissions granted to Gideon becomes its own extended discussion.

summary.principle: Animals disqualified from the altar — through bestiality, idol worship, prostitute's payment, or physical defect — contaminate any mixture in any quantity, each exclusion is carefully derived from its own phrase in Leviticus 1:2 (since simple logical inference repeatedly fails), and even a Torah hero's night of destroying idolatry required extraordinary, explicitly enumerated exceptions.

flowSteps.content: 🚫 New mishna: disqualified animals ruin a mixture in ANY amount, unlike ordinary halakhic mixtures
🔄 Distinguished from parallel mishnayot by timing (before/after consecration) and severity (forbidden-to-use vs. merely disqualified)

columns.content: ⚖️ A fortiori inferences for robe'a/nirva repeatedly fail, refined case by case
📜 Each exclusion tied to its own precise phrase in the verse

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: disqualification from the altar for moral/ritual reasons is uniquely severe — never nullified by a majority, however small the disqualified portion

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens if even ONE disqualified animal (e.g., one used in bestiality) becomes mixed into a large group of otherwise fit sacrificial animals?
o: The disqualified animal is simply removed and the rest remain fit
The entire mixture, in any quantity, becomes prohibited from the altar — it is never nullified by a majority
Nothing changes; disqualification doesn't transfer through mixtures
Only half the group is disqualified
quiz.e: The mishna's central ruling is that these categories of disqualified animals contaminate an entire mixture regardless of ratio, unlike typical halakhic mixtures where a minority can be nullified by a majority.

quiz.q: According to Rav Shimi bar Ashi, what key distinction separates this mishna from the parallel one in tractate Zevaḥim about mixtures being forbidden?
o: There is no real distinction; they are identical
This mishna addresses animals that became intermingled while still NON-SACRED (before consecration); the Zevaḥim mishna addresses animals already consecrated when mixed
This mishna only applies to birds
The Zevaḥim mishna only applies outside Eretz Yisrael
quiz.e: Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains that the two mishnayot cover different timing scenarios — one for animals mixed before consecration, one for animals already consecrated when mixed — making both rulings necessary.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject the simple a fortiori inference that bestiality-involved animals should be disqualified just like blemished ones (based purely on 'transgression')?
o: Because bestiality is not actually forbidden
Because an ox that plowed together with a donkey (a real transgression) remains fully fit for the altar — proving transgression alone doesn't disqualify an animal
Because blemished animals are never disqualified
Because the inference is never challenged
quiz.e: The counter-example of plowing with an ox and donkey (a genuine prohibited act) shows that mere involvement in a transgression doesn't automatically disqualify an animal from the altar, forcing a more refined analysis (capital-level transgressions, witnessed by two people).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon, why does the Torah need to separately exclude BOTH an animal used in bestiality (rove'a) AND an animal that gored a person (noge'ach), rather than inferring one from the other?
o: They are actually the same case
Each has a unique stringency the other lacks — bestiality counts even if forced, while a goring animal's owner pays a ransom (not applicable to bestiality)
The Torah never actually excludes noge'ach
There's no reason; it's arbitrary repetition
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon explains that each case has a distinguishing legal feature not shared by the other, so neither exclusion can be inferred from the other — both need their own explicit textual source.

quiz.q: According to Rava's explanation of Gideon's bullock, how could it have been actually worshipped if worship-related consecration should disqualify it?
o: It was never actually worshipped at all
It was one of eight normally-forbidden acts specially and temporarily permitted to Gideon that night, per Rabbi Abba bar Kahana
The Torah's rules didn't apply before the Temple was built
Gideon was a priest, so special rules applied
quiz.e: Rava explains this was an extraordinary, one-time exception — Rabbi Abba bar Kahana lists eight normally-prohibited acts (including slaughtering outside the Tabernacle, at night, by a non-priest) that were specially permitted to Gideon that single night.
